concepts.title: Production Function
concepts.definition: The production function maps each combination of inputs, labour and capital, to the largest output technically obtainable from it, so it always describes efficient production under a given state of technology.
concepts.key_idea: Given technology, the function states the ceiling on output from any input mix - no more is possible from the same inputs.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec203.txt, section 3.1, equation 3.1 and Table 3.1, pages 37-38
question_patterns: explain what a production function of a firm shows
state the relation between labour capital and maximum output
why does a production function describe only efficient production
what happens to the production function when technology improves
from an input output table find the largest output for a given input pair
name the factors of production used by a firm in the simple model

solution_steps.action: Identify the inputs and the output
solution_steps.explain: The two factors are labour and capital; the function assigns to each pair the maximum output q.
Since q is a maximum, no input mix can yield more, which is exactly what efficiency means here.
The whole mapping rests on current technology; better technology rewrites the function, raising output for every mix.

concepts.title: Short Run and Long Run
concepts.definition: The short run is any period in which at least one factor stays fixed and output can be raised only by varying the other factor; the long run is long enough for every factor to be varied, so no fixed factor remains.
concepts.formula: time_horizon = fixed_factor_present (short run) versus all_factors_variable (long run)
concepts.key_idea: Run length is defined by factor flexibility, not by calendar days or months.
question_patterns: why is the long run not defined as a fixed number of months
state the law of diminishing marginal product with a farming example
what makes a factor fixed or variable
give an example of adjusting output when capital cannot change
which factors can a firm vary in the long run
how does the definition of the two runs differ across industries

solution_steps.explain: If some factor cannot be changed in time to alter output, the firm is in the short run.
The unchangeable input is the fixed factor; the adjustable one is the variable factor.

solution_steps.action: Define the long run by reach
solution_steps.explain: When every input, plant and machine included, can be varied, the horizon is the long run.

concepts.title: Isoquant
concepts.definition: An isoquant collects every input combination of labour and capital that yields the same maximum output, acting as the producer's counterpart of the consumer's indifference curve; with positive marginal products it slopes downward.
concepts.key_idea: One curve, one output level: many labour-capital mixes can bake the same-sized cake.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec203.txt, section 3.2, isoquant box and diagram, pages 39-40
question_patterns: define an isoquant and its analogy with indifference curves
list the input mixes that lie on the isoquant for ten units of output
why does an isoquant slope downward
what does moving to a higher isoquant mean
label an isoquant map for three output levels
how can the same output follow from different labour capital ratios

solution_steps.explain: Choose a target output and gather all labour-capital pairs that produce exactly it efficiently.
Because both factors contribute positively, less of one must be offset by more of the other, giving the negative slope.
Curves farther from the origin carry larger output labels, mirroring higher indifference curves.

concepts.title: Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product
concepts.definition: Holding other inputs constant, total product links each amount of the variable input to the output obtained, average product spreads that output over the units of input, and marginal product is the extra output from one more unit of the input.
concepts.key_idea: Total is the schedule, average is output per worker, and marginal is the addition from the latest worker.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec203.txt, sections 3.3.1 to 3.3.3, equations 3.2 to 3.4 and Table 3.2, pages 40-41
question_patterns: compute average product and marginal product from a total product schedule
total product rises from 24 to 40 as labour rises from 2 to 3, find the marginal product
define output per unit of the variable input
how is total product built from the marginal products of successive units
find the addition to output when one more worker is employed
complete an average and marginal product table from total output data

solution_steps.explain: Dividing total product by the number of variable-input units gives the average product.
Dividing the change in total product by the change in input gives the marginal product of the input.

worked_examples.question: Using Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product, compute the result for total_product = 3, units_of_variable_input = 3, change_in_total_product = 3, change_in_input = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Spread output over the input: average_product = total_product / units_of_variable_input = 1.0 Step 2: Measure the latest addition: marginal_product = change_in_total_product / change_in_input = 1.5 Final result: 1.5

worked_examples.question: Using Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product, compute the result for total_product = 4, units_of_variable_input = 4, change_in_total_product = 4, change_in_input = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Spread output over the input: average_product = total_product / units_of_variable_input = 1.0 Step 2: Measure the latest addition: marginal_product = change_in_total_product / change_in_input = 1.333333 Final result: 1.333333

concepts.title: Law of Variable Proportions (Diminishing Marginal Product)
concepts.definition: As more units of one factor are added to fixed amounts of the others, its marginal product first rises, then falls; the rise reflects better factor proportions, the fall the crowding of the variable factor on the fixed one.
concepts.formula: marginal_product_pattern = rise_then_fall as variable input increases
concepts.key_idea: Changing proportions first help, then hurt: too little labour wastes land, too much crowds it.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec203.txt, section 3.4, farmer and land example, pages 41-42
question_patterns: state the law of variable proportions with a farming example
why does marginal product rise before it falls
explain the crowding that drives down the marginal product
what are factor proportions and how do they change
when does the fixed factor become a bottleneck for workers
relate the law of diminishing marginal product to changing input ratios

solution_steps.explain: Vary only labour against fixed land, so the input ratio keeps shifting.
Initially each extra worker has more of the fixed factor to work with, so marginal product climbs.
Beyond a point workers outnumber the land they can till efficiently, so each adds less and marginal product declines.

concepts.title: Shapes of TP, MP and AP Curves and their Mutual Relation
concepts.definition: Total product rises at an increasing then decreasing rate, while marginal and average product curves are inverse U-shaped; marginal product leads average product - average rises while marginal lies above it, falls once marginal drops below, and marginal cuts average at its peak.
concepts.formula: mp_above_ap implies ap rising; mp_below_ap implies ap falling
concepts.key_idea: The average follows the marginal: whichever way the marginal sits relative to it decides the average's direction.
question_patterns: describe the shapes of the total average and marginal product curves
why does the marginal product curve cut the average product curve at its maximum
when does average product rise even while marginal product is falling
sketch the inverse U pattern of average and marginal returns
what happens to total product when marginal product turns negative
why must average equal marginal for the very first unit of input

solution_steps.explain: Total product climbs throughout while marginal product is positive, steepening first and then flattening.
An average rises whenever the marginal addition exceeds it and falls whenever the marginal falls short.
The two meet exactly at average product's maximum, which is why the marginal curve slices the average from above there.

concepts.title: Returns to Scale
concepts.definition: Scaling all inputs by the same proportion t may raise output in the same proportion (constant returns), a larger proportion (increasing returns), or a smaller one (decreasing returns); for the Cobb-Douglas form the sum of the exponents decides which case holds.
concepts.key_idea: Doubling everything may exactly double output, more than double it, or less - and the exponent sum tells which.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec203.txt, section 3.6, returns to scale and Cobb-Douglas box, pages 43-44
question_patterns: define constant increasing and decreasing returns to scale
what happens to output when all inputs are doubled in each returns case
write the condition on exponents for a Cobb-Douglas function to show constant returns
test a production function like two times L squared K squared for its returns behaviour
why can returns to scale be discussed only in the long run
compare scaling of inputs with varying one input alone

solution_steps.explain: Multiply labour and capital by the same factor t greater than one.

solution_steps.action: Compare output with the scale factor
solution_steps.explain: Output rising by t is constant returns, by more than t is increasing returns, by less is decreasing returns.
For q as x1 power alpha times x2 power beta, alpha plus beta equal to, above or below one matches the three cases.

concepts.title: Cost Function: Total Fixed, Total Variable and Total Cost
concepts.definition: For each output the firm picks the cheapest input combination, and in the short run its cost splits into a fixed part that does not vary with output and a variable part that does, their sum being total cost.
concepts.key_idea: Fixed cost is the price of standing ready; variable cost grows with every extra unit produced.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec203.txt, sections 3.7 and 3.7.1, equation 3.6 and Table 3.3, pages 44-45
question_patterns: how are total cost total fixed cost and total variable cost related
what does the firm's cost function show
find total cost at an output when fixed and variable costs are given
why is total cost at zero output equal to the fixed cost
which cost heads rise as production expands
why does the firm pick the least cost input combination for each output

solution_steps.explain: Total cost is the fixed outlay plus the variable outlay at that output.

worked_examples.question: Using Cost Function: Total Fixed, Total Variable and Total Cost, compute the result for total_fixed_cost = 3, total_variable_cost = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Add the two cost heads: total_cost = total_fixed_cost + total_variable_cost = 6.0 Final result: 6.0

worked_examples.question: Using Cost Function: Total Fixed, Total Variable and Total Cost, compute the result for total_fixed_cost = 4, total_variable_cost = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Add the two cost heads: total_cost = total_fixed_cost + total_variable_cost = 8.0 Final result: 8.0

concepts.title: Average Costs: SAC, AVC and AFC
concepts.definition: Per-unit costs divide each total by output: short run average cost equals total cost over output, average variable cost equals variable cost over output, and average fixed cost equals fixed cost over output, with average cost exactly the sum of the other two.
concepts.key_idea: Every per-unit figure is its total spread over output, and the averages stack up to the full unit cost.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec203.txt, section 3.7.1, equations 3.7 to 3.10 and Table 3.3, page 45
question_patterns: compute average cost average variable cost and average fixed cost from totals
show that average cost equals average variable plus average fixed cost
why does average fixed cost keep falling as output grows
what shape does the average fixed cost curve take
at one unit of output fixed cost is 20 and variable cost 10, give the per-unit figures
divide each total cost item by output to build the average schedule

solution_steps.explain: Divide total variable cost by output for the average variable cost.
Divide total fixed cost by output for the average fixed cost, which shrinks as output grows.
The sum of the two averages is the short run average cost of production.

worked_examples.question: Using Average Costs: SAC, AVC and AFC, compute the result for total_variable_cost = 3, output = 3, total_fixed_cost = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Spread the variable cost: average_variable_cost = total_variable_cost / output = 1.0 Step 2: Spread the fixed cost: average_fixed_cost = total_fixed_cost / output = 1.0 Step 3: Add the per-unit figures: short_run_average_cost = average_variable_cost + average_fixed_cost = 2.0 Final result: 2.0

worked_examples.question: Using Average Costs: SAC, AVC and AFC, compute the result for total_variable_cost = 4, output = 4, total_fixed_cost = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Spread the variable cost: average_variable_cost = total_variable_cost / output = 1.0 Step 2: Spread the fixed cost: average_fixed_cost = total_fixed_cost / output = 1.0 Step 3: Add the per-unit figures: short_run_average_cost = average_variable_cost + average_fixed_cost = 2.0 Final result: 2.0

concepts.title: Short Run Marginal Cost
concepts.definition: Marginal cost is the addition to total cost from producing one more unit; since fixed cost cannot change in the short run, this addition is entirely the change in variable cost, and summing marginal costs up to any output rebuilds the total variable cost.
concepts.key_idea: The cost of one more unit is the step in total cost, and every step is variable cost in disguise.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec203.txt, section 3.7.1, equations 3.11 and 3.12 and Table 3.3, pages 45-46
question_patterns: calculate marginal cost between two output levels from a total cost table
total cost rises from 49 to 53 as output rises from 4 to 5, find the marginal cost
why is short run marginal cost the same as the rise in variable cost
how does summing marginal costs recover the total variable cost

add up successive marginal costs to obtain the variable cost schedule

solution_steps.action: Take the cost step per unit
solution_steps.explain: Dividing the change in total cost by the change in output gives the marginal cost of the extra units.

worked_examples.question: Using Short Run Marginal Cost, compute the result for change_in_total_cost = 3, change_in_output = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Take the cost step per unit: marginal_cost = change_in_total_cost / change_in_output = 1.0 Final result: 1.0

worked_examples.question: Using Short Run Marginal Cost, compute the result for change_in_total_cost = 4, change_in_output = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Take the cost step per unit: marginal_cost = change_in_total_cost / change_in_output = 1.0 Final result: 1.0

concepts.title: Shapes of Short Run Cost Curves
concepts.definition: Fixed cost is a horizontal line and average fixed cost a rectangular hyperbola; variable-cost-driven curves are U-shaped - marginal, average variable and average cost all fall, bottom out and rise, and the marginal curve pierces each average curve from below exactly at its minimum.
concepts.formula: smc_below_avc implies avc falling; smc_above_avc implies avc rising
concepts.key_idea: Averages chase the marginal, so the marginal curve crosses each average at its lowest point.
question_patterns: describe the shapes of the short run marginal average variable and average cost curves
why does the marginal cost curve cut the average variable cost curve at its minimum
why does average fixed cost take the form of a rectangular hyperbola
where does the marginal cost curve meet the average cost curve and why
why is the minimum of average cost to the right of the minimum of average variable cost
relate the U shape of cost curves to the law of variable proportions

solution_steps.explain: Fixed cost stays flat, variable cost rises with output, and total cost rides parallel above it by the fixed amount.
While marginal cost sits below an average cost, that average falls; once above, the average rises.
Marginal cost crosses average variable cost and average cost from below precisely at their minima, and the average cost trough lies farther right because falling fixed cost delays its rise.

concepts.title: Long Run Costs and their Returns-to-Scale Link
concepts.definition: With every input variable there is no fixed cost, so long run average and marginal costs describe the same total; increasing returns pull average cost down, decreasing returns push it up, and constant returns hold it flat, giving both curves their U shape with marginal cutting average at its minimum.
concepts.key_idea: The long run average cost curve is the returns-to-scale story told in rupees per unit.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec203.txt, section 3.7.2, equations 3.13 and 3.14 and figure 3.9, pages 49-50
question_patterns: why is there no fixed cost in the long run
how do returns to scale shape the long run average cost curve
which returns to scale operate at the minimum point of long run average cost
state the relation between long run marginal cost and long run average cost
why do both long run cost curves look U shaped
explain why average cost falls under increasing returns and rises under decreasing returns

solution_steps.explain: All inputs vary in the long run, so total cost and variable cost coincide and only average and marginal curves remain.
Increasing returns make each unit cheaper as scale grows, decreasing returns dearer, and constant returns leave unit cost unchanged.
Average cost bottoms out exactly where constant returns hold, with marginal cost passing through that minimum from below.
